body.objective: Students will be able to choose and research a theme.
body.iCan: I can choose and research a theme.
successCriteria: I can choose a personal theme with depth
I can research the theme visually and through artists
I can plan a cohesive series of related works
body.hook: When Emily Carr painted the forests of British Columbia again and again, each painting stood alone, but together they told a bigger story. A series lets an artist explore one idea more deeply than any single work can.

vocabulary.definition: A big idea that connects a body of work.
A group of related artworks exploring one theme.
Collecting images, sketches and references about a theme.
The quality that makes works in a series look and feel connected.
Repeating an idea with changes to explore it further.
Studying how other artists have approached similar themes.

study.title: Building a Body of Work
study.question: How do artists explore one idea across a series?
study.passage:
Part 1, Theme brainstorm (10 minutes): List ten possible themes from your life and interests (for example home, change, identity, water, city at night, inherited objects, growth). Rate each: How much do I care? How many images can I imagine?
Part 2, Narrow (5 minutes): Choose one theme. Write a question it raises, for example "What does home mean when you've moved countries?"
Part 3, Research (20 minutes): Gather ten visual references (photos you take, sketches from life, found images) and research two artists who worked in series, for example Emily Carr (BC forests), Monet (haystacks), Kent Monkman or Cindy Sherman. Note how they kept the series connected.
Part 4, Plan cohesion (10 minutes): Decide what will stay the same across works (medium, size, palette, viewpoint or subject) and what will change.
Part 5, Series map (10 minutes): Sketch thumbnails for three to five works and arrange them in order.

examples.title: Weak vs strong theme
examples.problem: Which is stronger: "cats" or "what it means to belong"?
examples.answer: "What it means to belong" offers more ways to explore
examples.explore: How could cats still connect to belonging?

examples.title: Cohesion
examples.problem: How could five works on "home" stay connected?
examples.answer: Same size, same palette and a recurring window motif

examples.title: Iteration
examples.answer: He changed time of day and season while keeping the subject
examples.explore: What could you change instead of light?

examples.title: Guiding question
examples.answer: "How does water connect my family across continents?"
examples.explore: How would this question shape your images?

practice.a: A big idea connecting a body of work.
A group of related works exploring one theme.
The quality that makes works feel connected.

practice.q: Name an artist who worked in series.
practice.a: Monet, Emily Carr or another valid example.

practice.q: Give two ways to keep a series cohesive.
practice.a: Same medium, size, palette, viewpoint or subject.
It focuses the series and gives it depth.
Photos, sketches from life, found images and artist studies.

practice.q: How do you choose a strong theme?
practice.a: One you care about that can produce many images.

practice.q: What did Emily Carr explore in series?
practice.a: The forests and Indigenous villages of British Columbia.
To learn approaches to series and cohesion.

practice.q: Can a series be too repetitive? Explain.
practice.a: Yes; without change, works add nothing new.

practice.q: How should a series develop from first to last work?
practice.a: It should deepen or shift the idea, not just repeat it.

practice.q: Turn "family" into a theme with a question.
practice.a: For example, "What do we inherit besides looks?"

practice.q: Why might an artist break their own cohesion rule in one work?
practice.a: To create emphasis or a turning point in the series.

Choosing a theme that is too narrow or too vague

items.q: Define series.
items.answer: A group of related artworks exploring one theme.

items.q: Define cohesion.
items.answer: The quality that connects works in a series.

items.q: Give two ways to make a series cohesive.
items.answer: Same palette, size, medium, viewpoint or subject.

items.q: Why turn a theme into a question?
items.answer: It focuses the work and adds depth.

items.q: What is the difference between a theme and a subject?
items.answer: A subject is what is shown; a theme is the bigger idea.

items.q: Name one artist who worked in series and what they explored.
items.answer: Answers vary, for example Monet and light.

items.q: Explain how a series can develop an idea further than a single work.
items.answer: Each work explores a new angle, building a fuller story.

items.q: Propose a theme, question and cohesion plan for a three-work series.
items.answer: Answers vary.
